text:
Prompt caching is one of the highest-leverage things to get right early, and the ordering question you're asking is exactly the right one — it's the whole ballgame.

## What it actually is

The Messages API is stateless. Every request sends the full prompt, and the model runs *prefill* over all of it — computing attention state for every token — before generating the first output token. On a 50K-token system prompt that's expensive and slow, and you pay for it identically on every request even though the bytes are identical.

Prompt caching stores that internal state (the KV cache) server-side, keyed by the exact bytes of the prompt prefix. On a hit, prefill is skipped for the cached span: you pay ~0.1× the input rate for those tokens and TTFT drops substantially.

The backend analogy that fits best: it's a **prefix-keyed memoization of prefill**, not an HTTP response cache. Nothing about the *response* is cached — only the work of reading the input.

## Why order matters: it's a prefix match, not a set match

This is the one invariant everything else follows from:

> The cache key is the exact byte sequence from the start of the prompt up to each breakpoint. A single byte differing at position N invalidates the cache for everything at position ≥ N.

The API renders your request in a fixed order:

```
tools  →  system  →  messages
```

So `tools` sits at position 0. If your tool list is built per-user, or serialized from a dict without sorted keys, or you add one tool mid-conversation, **nothing downstream caches** — the system prompt and the entire conversation history are re-prefilled at full price, no error, no warning.

The design rule is therefore: **sort content by how often it changes, and make the physical order match.**

| Position | Content | Changes |
|---|---|---|
| tools | deterministic, sorted tool list | never |
| system | frozen instructions, few-shot examples, retrieved docs | never / per-session |
| messages (early) | conversation history | append-only |
| messages (tail) | the current question, timestamps, request IDs | every request |

The classic mistake is interpolating `f"Current date: {datetime.now()}"` into the top of the system prompt. That's ~10 tokens that make the other 50K uncacheable forever. Same for a session UUID, a per-user name, or a conditional `if flag: system += ...` section (each flag combination becomes its own distinct prefix).

## Breakpoints

You mark where the cacheable prefix ends with `cache_control` on a content block:

```json
"system": [
  {"type": "text", "text": "<50K of stable instructions>",
   "cache_control": {"type": "ephemeral"}}
]
```

A marker on the last system block caches tools + system together, since tools render first.

- **Max 4 breakpoints per request.**
- Goes on any content block: system text, tool definitions, `text` / `image` / `tool_result` / `document` in messages.
- **Minimum cacheable prefix is model-dependent** and *not* monotonic across generations — 512 tokens on Opus 5, 1024 on Opus 4.8 / Sonnet 5, but 4096 on Opus 4.6 and Haiku 4.5. Below the minimum it silently doesn't cache: no error, just `cache_creation_input_tokens: 0`.

The placement trap worth internalizing: if requests share a big preamble but differ in the final question, put the breakpoint at the end of the **shared** part, not the end of the prompt. A breakpoint after the varying tail writes a unique cache entry per request that is never read back — a pure surcharge.

```json
"messages": [{"role": "user", "content": [
  {"type": "text", "text": "<shared context>", "cache_control": {"type": "ephemeral"}},
  {"type": "text", "text": "<varying question>"}
]}]
```

There's also top-level automatic caching (`cache_control` as a request-level field) which auto-places one breakpoint on the last cacheable block and advances it as the conversation grows. Good default for multi-turn chat; wrong tool when your prompt ends in per-request content, or when different sections change at different rates.

## TTL

- `{"type": "ephemeral"}` → **5 minutes** (default)
- `{"type": "ephemeral", "ttl": "1h"}` → **1 hour**

A read refreshes the timer for free. The lifetime is measured from the **start** of the writing/reading request, so generation time counts against it — a 4-minute generation leaves ~1 minute of headroom on a 5-minute entry.

Pick by the start-to-start gap between requests sharing the prefix: under 5 min → 5-minute TTL (continuous traffic keeps it warm indefinitely, and the 1h TTL buys nothing but a doubled write price); 5–60 min → 1-hour; over an hour → neither, re-warm on a schedule or eat the miss.

## Pricing

- **Cache write:** 1.25× base input (5-min TTL), 2× (1-hour TTL)
- **Cache read:** ~0.1× base input

Break-even: with 5-min TTL, two requests (1.25 + 0.1 = 1.35× vs 2× uncached). With 1-hour TTL, three (2 + 0.2 = 2.2× vs 3×). Writes only bill the delta past the highest cache hit, so a healthy multi-turn loop writes only what the last turn appended.

On the Claude API, cache reads also don't count against input-token rate limits on most models — so this raises effective throughput, not just cost.

## Verify it, and keep verifying it

```python
resp.usage.cache_read_input_tokens      # served from cache (~0.1×)
resp.usage.cache_creation_input_tokens  # written this request (1.25×/2×)
resp.usage.input_tokens                 # the uncached remainder ONLY
```

Total prompt size is the sum of all three — `input_tokens` alone is misleading.

If `cache_read_input_tokens` is zero across repeated requests with what should be identical prefixes, a silent invalidator is at work. The usage fields tell you *that* the prefix broke, not where; to localize it, log consecutive request bodies and diff adjacent pairs — the previous request's full prompt should reappear byte-identical as a prefix of the next. (Strip `cache_control` markers before diffing; the moving marker always differs and is not an invalidator.)

The failure mode that actually costs money in production is a **regression**, not a bad initial implementation: caching works when you write it, then six months later someone adds a dynamic field to the system prompt and every request misses. Nothing errors — the bill just goes up. Worth a standing integration-test assertion that a second identical request shows `cache_read_input_tokens > 0`.

## Two refinements that surprise people

**Invalidation is tiered, not all-or-nothing.** There are three caches (tools, system, messages) and a change only invalidates its own tier and below. Changing `tool_choice` per request keeps the tools+system cache. Appending a message never touches tools or system. Only tool-definition changes and model switches force a full rebuild — caches are model-scoped, so a "cheap model for easy requests" cascade forfeits cache reuse across models and is often a net loss.

**Concurrent requests don't share a write.** An entry is readable only after the first response *begins streaming*. Fire N parallel requests with the same prefix and all N pay full price. For fan-out: send one, await the first streamed token, then fire the rest.

---

Two things worth knowing exist, for when you hit them: `max_tokens: 0` requests do prefill-only and return immediately, which is the supported way to pre-warm or keep an entry alive; and on Opus 5 / Opus 4.8 / Fable 5.x you can append `{"role": "system", ...}` messages *inside* `messages[]` to deliver mid-conversation operator instructions without invalidating the cached history — editing top-level `system` would re-prefill the entire conversation.

You asked a conceptual question rather than for a change, so there's nothing for me to implement here — no plan file written. If you want, point me at your prompt-assembly code and I'll audit it for silent invalidators and propose breakpoint placement.
